h1: A career as a whisky warehouse manager
title: A Career as a Whisky Warehouse Manager | Craft Beer School
desc: What a whisky warehouse manager does, the skills the job needs and how the role works in India's heat and excise system.
teaser: Thousands of casks, years of value and an excise officer who wants every litre accounted for. Welcome to the warehouse.
standfirst: Whisky spends most of its life in a warehouse, not a still. The person who runs that warehouse looks after the single largest asset a distillery owns. It is a quiet job until something goes wrong.
sections:
A malt distillery might run its stills for a few hours a day. Its warehouses hold every litre it has made for the past three, five or twelve years. That stock is the company's future sales. A warehouse manager is the custodian of it.

The job sounds static. It is not. Casks arrive from the filling store, move between racks, get sampled, regauged, re-racked, blended and sent to bottling. Each movement has to be recorded against a cask number, a fill date, a strength and a volume. Lose track of one cask and the stock records stop matching reality.

• Receiving. New casks arrive filled, often at a strength near 63.5% ABV. The manager checks the cask number, fill volume, strength and spirit type match the filling records.
  • Storage planning. Deciding where each cask goes. Floor level and top tier casks mature differently because temperature varies with height.
  • Sampling and inspection. Drawing samples with a valinch for the blender, checking for leaks, weeping staves and loose hoops.
  • Stock checks. Periodic counts and regauging to measure what has been lost to evaporation.
  • Excise. Keeping bonded stock records that satisfy the state excise department, which treats the warehouse as a store of untaxed spirit.
  • Safety. A warehouse full of high strength spirit is a fire risk. Ignition control, housekeeping and forklift discipline are daily concerns.

In Scotland, the angels' share is commonly quoted at around 2% of volume a year. In much of India, losses run well above that because of heat. The figure varies a great deal by site, warehouse design and cask position, so a good manager measures it rather than assumes it. Our guide to designing a whisky warehouse for Indian heat covers the building side.

Heat also changes what happens to strength. In humid Scottish warehouses, strength tends to fall over time. In hot, dry conditions water can leave faster than alcohol, so strength may hold or even rise. Monsoon humidity then pushes the other way. The manager who tracks volume and strength separately, cask by cask, understands the stock. The one who tracks only cask counts does not.
Skills that make a good manager

The best warehouse managers combine three things: physical knowledge of casks, comfort with data and calm with regulators.

Cask knowledge means being able to spot a leaker by the dark stain on a stave, knowing the difference between a hogshead and a butt by sight and understanding what a cask's history means for the blender. Data comfort means trusting the cask management system while checking it regularly against the racks. Regulatory calm means keeping records clean enough that an excise inspection is routine.

People skills matter more than the title suggests. Warehouse teams work with forklifts, heavy casks and spirit vapour. A manager who keeps the team careful keeps them safe.

Few people start as warehouse managers. Common routes in are through warehouse operative or cask handling roles, through a distillery QC lab or from logistics and inventory work in another industry. Supply chain and stores experience from fast moving goods transfers well, as long as you learn the excise side.

Formal qualifications help without being essential. The General Certificate in Distilling from the Institute of Brewing and Distilling gives a solid grounding in the whole process. Knowing how the spirit was made makes you better at protecting it. Our guide to whisky maturation and casks is a good starting point for the science.
The numbers a manager lives by

Warehouse work runs on litres of pure alcohol (LPA), not litres of liquid. A 200 litre barrel filled at 63.5% ABV holds 127 LPA. A 250 litre hogshead at the same strength holds about 159 LPA. Excise records, stock valuations and blending plans all use LPA because strength changes over time while the alcohol is what carries the value and the duty.

A manager reports a handful of numbers every month: casks held, LPA held, LPA lost since the last check, casks found leaking and casks moved to bottling. When the loss figure for one warehouse jumps, the manager is the first to ask why. It might be a run of hot weeks, a roof that has lost insulation or a batch of casks with weak staves. Finding the cause early saves spirit that would otherwise disappear into the air.

Warehouse managers sit close to the blender and the operations director. Over time, many move into broader operations roles, inventory planning or stock management for a group of sites. Some move toward blending, because years of nosing samples from every corner of the warehouse is a quiet sensory training of its own.

If the role appeals, start by learning the life of a cask from filling to bottling. Write down every step a cask goes through and who touches it at each stage. If you cannot fill in the distillation and filling steps with confidence, that is the gap to close first.
faqs: What does a whisky warehouse manager do?
They look after maturing casks: receiving, storing, sampling, inspecting and tracking every cask, keeping excise records accurate and running a safe warehouse.
Do I need a distilling qualification to manage a warehouse?
Not always, but a grounding such as the IBD General Certificate in Distilling helps you understand the stock you are protecting.
Why do whisky losses run higher in India?
Heat speeds evaporation through the cask, so the yearly loss is well above the figure commonly quoted for Scotland. It varies widely by site and should be measured.
